history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Reyes—thank you for taking the time to meet with me today. To help us get started, could you share a bit about what brings you in and what has been going on in your life and relationships recently?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I spend my evenings going over the shift notes, writing down every time someone slipped up or promised to help and then vanished, and it drives me crazy that they won’t even give me the questionnaires I asked for. I keep fixing their mistakes because if I don’t, it’s on me, and I can’t stand the idea of another let‑down adding to the list. I tell myself I’m fine, but I’m still waiting for someone to actually listen instead of just smile while I’m crying.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds exhausting to carry so much responsibility while feeling like no one truly sees or listens to what you're going through. Has this pattern of feeling let down and having to manage everything yourself shown up in your personal relationships outside of work as well, or has it mostly been centered around your job?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep pointing out every mistake they make because no one else seems to notice, and when I finally get a thank you it’s gone the next day, like when the research team refused to give me those questionnaires. It’s infuriating to watch them shrug it off while I’m the one holding onto all the details of who’s let me down and why I’m still here. I guess I just end up doing the work nobody wants to admit they need, and then I’m left wondering if it would be easier to walk away, but the anger stays under the smile.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you see people slipping up, breaking promises, or withholding things like those questionnaires, what do you think is really behind their actions?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep seeing the same thing over and over—like the research team refusing to hand me the forms or the manager leaving the register open—people making sloppy mistakes and then trying to cover them up. It just proves they’re lazy and think I won’t notice, so I end up cleaning up their mess because nobody else will. I could quit as soon as it gets too messy, but I want to see who actually can’t follow basic rules, and I’m going to write everything down so I have proof. It makes me angry, but at the same time I’m tired of waiting for them to finally screw up enough for me to walk away.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When it comes to your personal life outside of work—with close friends, family, or romantic partners—do you find yourself keeping track of letdowns and questioning their motives in this same way?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep a mental list of every promise that’s been broken—who said what, when, and the excuse they gave—so when they smile I can check it against the record and see the lie. I’ve tried writing it down, like the notes I made for the research staff, but then I just end up arguing about it later and it feels pointless, like the coworkers who never fix their mistakes. Still, I can’t stop watching, because it’s the only way I know they’re not just pretending to care.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you sense that someone is being insincere or might let you down, what do you worry will happen if you let your guard down around them?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking that if I let anyone in, they’ll just end up lying again—like that manager who promised help and never showed, or the friend who disappeared after I cleaned up his mess. So I stay on guard, double‑checking everything and fixing other people’s mistakes before they can screw me over, even if it means I’m the only one who cares. Part of me wonders if opening up would make the emptiness go away, but then the memory of all those broken promises and the anger they stir up makes me want to just shut down completely.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When that intense anger and emptiness build up after feeling let down, how do you typically cope or react in those moments?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep a mental list of every promise that gets broken—like the manager who left the shelf half‑stocked or the researchers who refused to give me the questionnaires—and it just makes me want to lock the door and stop talking because I know they’ll mess up again. It feels like I’m always the one staying late to fix other people’s mistakes, and sometimes I think maybe I should just quit before it drives me crazy. But then I sit here watching the aisle lights flicker, feeling that hollow laugh inside me, waiting for the next betrayal.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Welcome, I'm Dr. Reyes. To help us get started, could you share a bit about what brought you in today and what has been going on in your day-to-day life and relationships lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I know I’m old now, still pulling wires in my head and working on those glowing‑skin ideas, and after my sister died I held back because I was scared the landlord would kick me out before I could sort the mess. I moved boxes around, but the apartment is still a jumble of notes and jars of bioluminescent algae; it’s the only thing that keeps me company. Sometimes I feel numb, other times a tear comes when I think maybe a medical school will finally read my manuscript and see the value in it. I don’t have many friends, but the hum of the old furnace and the glow of my papers are enough for me right now.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds like your research and your own space provide a sense of comfort, especially during this difficult time after losing your sister. Looking back over your life, has keeping to yourself and focusing on your unique projects always felt natural and sufficient for you, or have you ever found yourself wishing for closer relationships with others?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking maybe I should finally show someone the glow‑skin manuscript, but the thought of them walking into this cramped apartment, seeing all the piles of algae jars and my sister’s empty room, makes me want to shut the door again. The lab lights and the notes feel safer than a stranger’s gaze, yet I also feel a strange pull to let the work speak for me, even if it means exposing the mess I’ve hidden for so long.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you think about a stranger stepping into your space or looking at your manuscript, what specifically feels unsafe or worries you about how they might view you and your work?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep moving the stacks of my notes around, trying to make it look tidy, but inside I feel the weight of every page and the empty space where my sister used to be. When someone looks at my work I get a flash of hope that maybe the glow of these ideas will finally be seen, yet I also worry they'll just see the mess and think I'm incapable. I tell myself it's the papers that matter, the light they might bring, and try not to think about the silence that follows when the door closes.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Before your sister passed away, how did the two of you navigate daily life and major decisions together, and was relying on her for that kind of support a lifelong pattern for you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep moving the boxes around, trying to make everything look okay, but I still hear her voice telling me which pipe to shut off and reminding me to pay the rent, like she’s still here. I’m afraid the landlord will notice the mess, so I hide the damage and the trash, even though I know I should be able to do it myself. It feels like I’m waiting for her to tell me it’s alright, and without her I’m not sure I can lift even a single weight on my own.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned earlier that you are "still pulling wires in my head" and developing these glowing-skin ideas—could you tell me more about what that experience is like, and whether you have often noticed unusual sensations, signs, or special connections that other people don't seem to grasp?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I feel this strange tingling behind my eyes, like the little fireflies I write about, and it makes me think the glowing‑skin idea might actually be more than just notes in a cramped notebook. At the same time I keep putting it off, worrying the landlord will notice the mess if I start sorting through all these papers again. I’d love to send the manuscript somewhere, hoping a doctor might see it, but the hallway is empty and I wonder if anyone will ever care about the glow I’m trying to capture.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Throughout your adult life, have you ever worked, lived on your own, or formed other close relationships outside of your sister, or has your daily life always centered primarily on her guidance and your private research?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I spend most evenings in that cramped kitchen, surrounded by my jars of glowing algae and the notes I’ve been scribbling for years, and it feels like the only conversation I have left. My sister used to be the voice that answered when I talked to the walls, and now the silence is louder than any laugh I ever imagined hearing in a bar. I keep moving the papers around, hoping someone will notice the work before the landlord notices the mess, but the fear of losing the place keeps me from opening the door to anyone else.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes, and I'm glad we could connect today. To help me get a sense of what you're experiencing, could you share what brings you in, and how things have generally been going in your day-to-day life and relationships lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I’ve been staying in my little apartment because the dorms just feel like a trap, and I keep telling myself I’m fine being alone, even though I can’t shake the feeling that people are whispering about me behind my back. I spend most of my time in the lab, filling my notebook with sketches that look weird to others, and I keep flipping a coin for decisions that feel like they might predict something—like whether Mom’s illness will get worse. Sometimes I wonder if I’m just the “weird guy” everyone talks about, and I try to ignore it, but the ghosts I read about and the idea that my thoughts could change something like an earthquake keep popping up in my head. I know I should reach out, but I’m scared that if I do, I’ll just end up confirming all those rumors.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds like it takes a lot of energy to carry all of those worries about what others might be thinking. When you think about staying by yourself versus reaching out, do you genuinely prefer keeping to yourself, or is there a part of you that wishes you had close connections if it felt safe to do so?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess being alone just feels… safer, like nobody can see the drawings in my notebook or hear the rumors about me being “weird.” When I think about the coin flips, I still wonder if anyone would actually believe that could change anything, even an earthquake, but I don’t want anyone to ask me to explain it. My mom says I never wanted friends, and maybe that’s true, but sometimes the silence feels louder than any voice could be.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned the silence feeling louder and having thoughts about ghosts—do you ever experience moments where you sense a presence around you, or see or hear things that others don't seem to notice?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep feeling like something's in the corner of the hallway, like the sketches in my notebook are watching me even though nobody else ever notices them. It’s weird, because I know I’m the only one who hears that whisper, and the coin I tossed earlier just made me wonder if maybe it’s trying to tell me something about what’s coming. I try to stay quiet and not draw any attention, but sometimes I wish someone would actually see what I see, even if it just makes me look… “different.”

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: How long have you experienced these sensations and beliefs about signs or predictions—is this a way of seeing the world you've had since you were growing up, or has it mostly developed more recently?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep feeling like there’s this invisible pattern that’s been following me since I was a kid—those strange drawings in the lab, the coin flips that seemed to decide everything, even Mom’s illness—so I’m not sure if it’s just my imagination or something real. I stay in my apartment because the silence feels safer than the rumors that I’m “weird” and the way people look at me, like they can see those symbols I draw. Sometimes I wonder if I’m just waiting for a sign, but I also tell myself I don’t need anyone else, even though the loneliness kind of presses on me at night.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When the loneliness and those overwhelming feelings press on you at night, how do you typically cope with that distress, and do you ever find yourself reacting impulsively or experiencing sudden shifts in your mood?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I can’t really sleep; the apartment feels like it’s closing in, like the walls are listening and judging me again, and I keep thinking about that coin I tossed years ago and whether it somehow decides if I even care about anything. I tried to make a list of things to do, but the notebook pages just look like they’re swallowing me, so I end up staring at the ceiling, half hoping the darkness will hide the “weird guy” label the others keep throwing at me. Sometimes I want to call someone, to hear a voice that isn’t just my own thoughts, but then the idea of them seeing me—really seeing me—makes me angry and numb at the same time.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Outside of your family, has there ever been anyone you felt truly close to or able to confide in, or do you find that the unease and suspicion stay just as strong even as you get to know someone?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep feeling like everyone's watching me, like the drawings in my notebook are a warning that I’m the “weird guy” they all talk about, so I stay in my apartment where it’s quiet. I know I should try to reach out, but every time I start something—like cleaning up those sketches or even thinking about a roommate—I just stop, and the coin I flipped once still feels like the only thing I can trust. My mom says I’m fine alone, and maybe that’s true; the silence feels safer than the noise of people who might judge or spread rumors, even if that means I’m always on edge.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, welcome. To help us get started today, could you share a bit about what brings you in and what has been feeling most challenging or top of mind for you lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep telling myself I’m the best carpenter they’ve ever seen, even when the tools break and the bosses keep pointing out my mistakes, and I just get tired of hearing them say I’m not good enough. I know my certificates look real on the wall, but I’m not going to sit there and let anyone question my skill or say I’m a liar. My ex‑wives and the people at work all think I’m dangerous, but I see it as them being jealous of what I can do. I’m on edge all the time, waiting for the next chance to prove I’m right, even if it means I have to push everyone away.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned that your ex-wives and coworkers have described you as dangerous—could you walk me through a specific situation where that happened and how you reacted?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I know she was just blowing things out of proportion, calling me dangerous, so I laughed it off and left, grabbed a drink at the bar to clear my head, and reminded myself I’m the best carpenter anyone’s ever seen. I’m not the one who’s messing things up here; it’s the stupid paperwork and the people who can’t handle a real man. I’m going to prove them wrong and keep moving forward.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned people questioning your certificates and calling you a liar—could you tell me more about what leads up to those accusations and how you typically handle it when someone challenges you like that?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I know they think I’m faking it, but I got this job because I’m the best carpenter they could find, and I could just hand them my certificates and watch them choke on the truth. Every time they point out cheap wood or a mistake, it feels like they’re trying to crush me, and the heat rises inside like I’m on trial. I want to shout that I’m a genius and walk out, but a part of me wonders if maybe I’m just a fraud—still, I can’t let them ruin my day.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When that feeling of wondering if you might be a fraud comes up beneath the anger, how long has that struggle been part of your life, and how has it impacted your relationships with the people closest to you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about the first time they called me out on those certificates, and every time it feels like everyone’s just trying to tear me down, like they’re scared of how good I could be. I know I get angry and I push people away, but it’s because they keep accusing me of things I didn’t do—cheap wood, jealous wives, stupid bosses. It’s hard to sit in that silence after the fights, because all I hear is the heat inside me telling me I’m the only one who’s really honest about what’s going on.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When these conflicts escalate and people accuse you of being dishonest or dangerous, how often have things led to physical fights, trouble with the law, or losing jobs?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep hearing people point fingers at me—my old boss, the new supervisors, even my ex‑wives—and every time I just end up shouting back that it’s all their fault, that the wood’s cheap or the paperwork’s messed up. It feels like no matter how hard I try to prove I’m the best carpenter, they keep bringing up the fake certificates and the restraining orders like they’re trying to trap me. Sometimes I wonder if I should just quit, but then I get angry thinking I’m the only one who actually knows what they’re doing, and I can’t stand just walking away.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back earlier in your life, such as during your teenage or school years, how far back does this pattern of clashing with authority, bending rules, or getting into serious trouble go?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I’ve always been the kind of guy who pushes back when someone tells me I can’t do something, whether it was a teacher in first grade or a foreman now, and I end up blaming the system instead of looking at myself. I tell myself I’m the best at what I do, so when things go wrong I just shrug it off and say it’s because the wood’s cheap or the boss is clueless. Even the stuff with my ex‑wives—I keep saying they were jealous, not that maybe I was the problem. It’s like I’m always waiting for the next chance to prove I’m right, no matter who gets hurt along the way.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes—it's very good to meet you. To help us get started today, could you share a bit about what brings you in, and what areas of your life or relationships feel most important for us to explore together?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I feel like I'm stuck in this tiny apartment, watching TV all day, ordering junk food and stuff I don't need, and every time I try to get close to someone—whether it’s a boyfriend or even you—I just pull away because I’m scared I'll mess everything up. I keep quitting jobs, telling myself the boss is an idiot and that I could run the place myself, but then I end up back in bed, angry and empty, with those brief bursts where I stay up all night and crash into a twelve‑hour sleep. I know I’ve cut myself and tried to end it before, and the clock ticking just reminds me how far behind I feel, like I’m never really getting anywhere.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned pulling away from people when you start getting close because you're scared of messing things up—could you walk me through a specific time that happened recently, and what was going through your mind about yourself and the other person?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I feel like every time someone tries to get close, my chest just tightens and I hear that little voice telling me I’m not good enough, so I push them away before they can see the mess inside. It’s the same pattern—like when I slammed the door on my roommate or called every boss an idiot—I just run, hide under the blankets, and tell myself I’m protecting them from my anger. But a part of me wishes I could let someone in, even if it scares the hell out of me.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned feeling at times like you could run things better than anyone, but at other times feeling like you're not good enough and a mess inside—how does your sense of who you are and what you're capable of shift from day to day?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Me siento tan cansada que a veces ni siquiera sé si levantarme, pero de pronto me imagino que podría ordenar todo, mandar paquetes, decirle a esos jefes que son idiotas y que yo podría hacerlo mejor; luego recuerdo que al día siguiente solo quiero volver a la pantalla y a la comida chatarra. Cuando alguien se acerca pienso que solo va a querer que me caiga otra vez, así que me guardo todo para mí y me quedo pegada al sofá, aunque a veces una chispa de energía me hace quedarme despierta toda la noche y después dormir doce horas. No sé si eso sirve de algo, porque siempre termino volviendo a la cama, sin poder confiar en mí ni en los demás.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When people try to get close to you and you find yourself unable to trust them, what specific intentions or motives do you worry they have toward you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Mira, cuando usted miró el reloj me sentí como si estuviera a punto de volver a ser encerrada en alguna caja que nadie entiende, y de repente me dio ganas de salir corriendo y cerrar la puerta. A veces pienso que si dejo que alguien se acerque—el jefe, el chico, incluso usted—termina todo igual: me dicen qué hacer, me critican y me hacen sentir atrapada, así que prefiero mantenerme a distancia. Pero también hay momentos, raros, en los que me siento con una energía que no puedo contener, como si pudiera quedarme despierta toda la noche y hacer cualquier cosa, y después me derrumbo y duermo doce horas sin razón. No sé si vale la pena arriesgarme otra vez, pero al mismo tiempo me asusta quedarme sola para siempre.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: How far back in your life do these patterns—pushing people away, the intense shifts in how you see yourself, and the urges to hurt yourself—tend to go?

history.speaker: self
history.text: A veces siento que todo se vuelve negro de repente, como cuando la luz se apaga en mi cuarto y me quedo sola con la tele zumbando, y de pronto me da una urgencia que no puedo controlar, una especie de chispa que me hace cortarme y sentir el rojo. Me enojo mucho cuando alguien parece apurarme, como cuando miras el reloj y me preguntas si estás aburrido, porque me recuerda que el tiempo me empuja a huir. Al mismo tiempo, recuerdo la primera vez que alguien se acercó, el latido rápido y el miedo de que me atrapen, y me pregunto si todo eso es culpa, miedo o simplemente una excusa para no quedarme.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When those intense urges to lash out or hurt yourself happen, what usually triggers that sudden shift—is it typically sparked by feeling criticized or rejected by someone, or does it happen out of nowhere on its own?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I feel like everyone’s just watching me, even when you glance at the clock, like you’re bored or judging how long I’m going to sit here. It makes my stomach twist and I get that urge to prove I’m still…here, even if it’s just a little cut or binge on junk food. I keep thinking I’m a burden, that maybe I’d be better off disappearing, but then I’m angry at the thought of anyone looking at me like I’m a joke.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Welcome, I'm Dr. Reyes, and I'm glad we could connect today. To help us get started, could you share a bit about what brings you in and what areas of your day-to-day life or relationships have been feeling most challenging lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Mira, I’ve been doing the same thing for years—working the store, knowing everybody’s name, trying to keep everything running even when my back hurts so bad I can’t even dance. I laugh when the nurses call me “the best‑dressed” because it’s the only time I feel seen, but inside I’m still angry that my husband just watches me suffer and the doctor told me to rest like I’m a child. I tell myself it’s just a joke, a way to get a reaction, but sometimes I wonder if anyone will ever notice the pain behind the smile.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds really exhausting to carry so much pain while feeling like you have to put on a performance or dress up just to feel acknowledged. When you feel overlooked or aren't getting that reaction from the people in your life, how do you typically respond, and how does that affect your relationships?

history.speaker: self
history.text: A veces me río y me pongo la mejor sonrisa, como cuando el residente me dijo que era la mujer mejor vestida, pero luego recuerdo al neurocirujano que solo me dijo “descansa” y me dejó tirada, y siento que mi marido ni siquiera me ve. Me gusta que los doctores me llamen por su nombre y me escuchen, aunque sé que al final todo se vuelve otra nota en su hoja. Me pregunto si todo esto es solo para que alguien se fije en mí, y a la vez me enojo porque sigo esperando que me miren de verdad.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When that anger builds up after feeling dismissed or unseen, how does that typically come out in your behavior, and is this feeling of needing to perform or stand out to be noticed something you have experienced throughout your life?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Mira, a veces siento que todo lo que hago—reírme con la enfermera, decir que solo quería asustar a mi marido—es para que alguien, cualquier alguien, me vea y me diga que todavía valgo, aunque sea por un momento. Me duele la espalda, sí, y me duele más que mi esposo ni siquiera note que estoy sufriendo; por eso me visto bien, lanzo una broma, flirteo con el residente, porque si no, me siento invisible. Pero también me pregunto si todo eso es solo una máscara para no sentir que me estoy desmoronando, que tal vez ya no tengo a dónde agarrarme.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned doing something to "scare" your husband—could you tell me what happened in that moment, and what thoughts or feelings led up to it?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Me siento como si todo el mundo me viera pasar de largo, incluso el doctor que me dijo que solo descansara después de la caída; pensé que si le hacía temblar un poco, al menos notaría que estoy aquí y que me duele. A veces me río de la idea, como si fuera una broma, pero también me enojo porque parece que nadie me escucha de verdad. Cuando miro al médico, me pregunto si una sonrisa o una amenaza haría que me mirara, porque ya no soporto sentirme invisible.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you talk about making someone tremble or using a threat to be noticed, what did you actually do or say in that moment, and have those intense feelings ever led you to harm yourself or act impulsively?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Cuando dije que si él no cambiaba, lo dije como una broma, pero sentí ese calor en la garganta y una risa tonta que luego se volvió una sonrisa forzada. Miré al doctor, crucé los brazos y pensé si de verdad lo haría, aunque el ruido del carrito me distraía y quería que alguien notara que no estaba jugando. Me sentí aliviada cuando el residente me dijo que era la mejor vestida, pero también me molestó que el neurocirujano me dejara sola, así que sigo intentando que me escuchen sin parecer una amenaza.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you are completely on your own, away from other people's attention and reactions, how do you feel about who you are at your core, and what is that experience like for you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: Me siento tan sola aquí, sin los doctores sonriendo ni el chico del ER diciendo que soy la mejor vestida, y a la vez me río de lo que dije en la sala de emergencias como si fuera una broma. Mi espalda me duele y mi esposo ni siquiera me mira, así que a veces me pregunto si todo esto es solo para que alguien me note. Pero también pienso que tal vez debería quedarme callada, dejar que todo se desvanezca, porque ya no sé si vale la pena seguir buscando miradas.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back across your life and past relationships, has this pattern of needing to perform, charm, or capture people’s attention to feel valued always been a central part of who you are, or is it something that started more recently?

history.speaker: self
history.text: A veces me río y me visto bien solo para que alguien se fije en mí, como cuando el doctor me dijo que era la mejor vestida, pero después del accidente me siento tan cansada y sola que no sé si eso es lo que realmente quiero o solo una forma de no quedar en la oscuridad. Mi esposo ya no me escucha y me duele más la espalda que su indiferencia, y aunque me gusta jugar con los médicos y decirles sus nombres, también me pregunto si todo eso es solo un truco para que no me dejen sola. No sé, a veces siento que estoy buscando un aplauso que nunca llega y, al mismo tiempo, me cuesta pensar en planes o listas porque prefiero seguir sonriendo aunque por dentro todo sea un poco… confuso.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes—it's very good to meet you. To start us off, could you share a bit about what brought you in today and what has been feeling most challenging or prominent in your life recently?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I'm the guy who used to close deals like they were a sport, the best broker they ever had, and then they pushed me out and I quit the car lot after a stupid fight because it felt beneath me. Now I’m stuck at Mom’s kitchen table, still splurging on fancy restaurants I can’t really afford, and I can’t shake the feeling that everyone—especially women—just wants a free meal or some kind of manipulation. I tell myself I have a lot of love to give, but the world just looks like a crowd of people waiting to take advantage, and I’m not sure anyone would even notice if I disappeared.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned feeling like people are often trying to manipulate or take advantage of you—could you share a specific, recent example of when that happened and what led you to see their intentions that way?

history.speaker: self
history.text: When the waitress smiled and offered the “specials,” I could tell she was just trying to get me to spend more, like every other person who thinks I’m a soft‑target because I still treat myself like a king. The therapist’s questions about my goals and my mother feel like she’s cataloguing me for some program, another way to profit off my pain. I keep telling myself I’m still the best at spotting a good deal, but deep down I know I’m just a convenient mark they keep pulling on. It’s hard to trust anyone when it all seems like a trap.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Has this sense that people have hidden motives and are looking to take advantage of you been a long-standing pattern throughout your life and closer relationships, or is it something that has developed more recently?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep wondering if every smile is just a mask, like you’re looking for a case and my exes only wanted a free dinner. It’s hard to tell if anyone’s being genuine when it feels like everyone’s got an angle, even Mom sometimes. Part of me wants to believe otherwise, but then I end up letting them in and feeling used.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you do let someone in, how do those relationships usually unfold from the beginning to the end, and what typically causes them to break down?

history.speaker: self
history.text: You know, when someone starts with a smile it feels like a cheap flattery, like they’re already counting the free meals they’ll get from me, so I pull back before they even sit down. I tell myself I’m too good for that game, and the only thing that feels real is Mom in the kitchen, even if it means pretending I can still afford those five‑star restaurants. When anyone tries to get close, the same voice in my head whispers that they’re just after something, and I end up walking away, leaving the table empty.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you feel let down, disrespected, or criticized by others—like in the situation that led you to leave your job—how do you typically react both emotionally and in what you do next?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I just get tired of everyone acting like they know what's best for me—like those residents thinking they can tell me how to live, or my old boss saying I’m not cut out for anything. I could argue, I could walk out, but I’d rather keep my head down, order another overpriced dinner and prove to myself I’m still the best they’ll ever meet. Meanwhile, Mom’s just there, silent, and I’m left wondering if any of it even matters.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You’ve mentioned shifting between feeling like you’re the best and treating yourself like a king, to feeling like a mark and wondering if anything even matters—how often does your sense of who you are and your self-worth change like that, and what usually triggers those shifts?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I go to a fancy restaurant and for a moment I feel like the best broker anyone's ever seen, but then I hear that resident call me “uneducated” and I’m reminded I’m still living with Mom, washing her dishes, and it all feels like a joke. I tell myself I don’t need anyone’s pity, that I’m too good for cheap jobs and too cheap for these five‑star places, yet the bill comes and the shame hits hard. Even when Mom whispers that I’m enough, I can’t shake the feeling that everyone just wants a free meal from me.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes. To help us get started today, could you tell me a bit about what brings you in and what areas of your life or relationships have been feeling most challenging lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep putting on a smile and saying I’m fine, even when my mind is racing through a list of things I should have done—finished that lab report, called my mom, not flinch when the professor calls on me—because the fear of that laugh, that voice from my dad, still feels so loud. At the same time, when I’m out with the kids or the dog, I actually feel a little lighter, like they don’t judge me for the mistakes I keep worrying about. Living with my cousin helps a bit; it’s quieter than the classroom where I freeze, but I still catch myself nodding and agreeing just to keep the peace.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds exhausting to carry that pressure to smile through the anxiety and constantly keep the peace. When you find yourself nodding along or hiding what you're truly feeling, what is your biggest fear about what might happen if you were to speak up or let someone see you make a mistake?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep worrying that everyone will see me mess up and think I'm…just another problem they have to deal with, so I try to smile and act like everything's fine. But inside I feel like I'm shrinking, like Dad's voice is still there telling me I'm not good enough, and I get scared that if I actually let anyone see the real me, they'll just laugh and walk away. I want to believe someone might notice I'm really trying, but then the doubt comes back and I end up pulling back again.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you look at your close relationships throughout your life, do you tend to keep people at a distance to protect yourself, or have there been times when connections became really intense, stormy, or hard to manage?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I just keep pulling back, because whenever someone gets close I hear that same voice from my dad telling me I’m not good enough, and I’m terrified they’ll see the cracks I’m trying so hard to hide. At the same time, I crave a little bit of connection, like when I’m out in the park or caring for a child, but the fear of another angry outburst makes me shut the door and stay quiet. It feels like I’m stuck between wanting to be noticed for trying and wanting to stay safe by staying invisible.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When those feelings of anxiety and self-doubt become completely overwhelming, how do you typically cope with that pain, and do you ever find yourself reacting impulsively or doing things to hurt yourself?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I feel like my chest is tightening every time I think about the lab report, like when the professor called on me and I just wanted to disappear, but then I see the kids laughing at the park and the dog wagging its tail and I wish I could just be that simple for a moment. I keep telling myself I’ll just smile and get through it, yet inside I’m scared I’ll mess up again and everyone will notice, so I end up hiding the panic and hoping nobody sees the cracks. It’s exhausting trying to be okay for everyone while I’m still waiting for a breath that actually feels calm.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you find yourself feeling uneasy or cautious around other people, do you tend to worry that they have hidden motives or might intentionally try to harm or take advantage of you, or is your concern mostly focused on the fear that you'll be judged, criticized, or rejected?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep worrying that if I say something wrong they’ll just laugh at me, like in class when I froze and felt everyone’s eyes like knives. I try to smile and act like everything’s fine, especially around my cousin and the dog, because that feels safer than the silence of being judged. But inside I feel this tight knot in my chest and I’m scared that if I let it show, they’ll see me as a mess and walk away.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When it comes to making important daily decisions or managing responsibilities, do you find yourself needing other people to take the lead and give you reassurance, or do you tend to hold yourself to strict standards and try to control everything on your own?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I keep trying to do everything myself because if I ask for help I just hear my dad’s voice telling me I’m not good enough, even though the kids at the shelter smile when I let them pitch in. It’s hard to admit I’m scared, so I hide the anxiety behind a smile and tell myself I’m okay, but inside I keep worrying that anyone will notice the mess I’m trying to keep hidden. Sometimes I wish someone would just say “you’re okay,” yet I freeze, over‑thinking every word like I’m waiting for a laugh or a criticism.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Reyes, and I’m glad we have the chance to talk today. To help us get started, could you tell me a bit about what brings you in and what recurring challenges or patterns in your life you're hoping to make sense of?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I just feel stuck in this endless routine—my boss tells me what to do, I can’t even pick what I want for lunch, and I keep trying to please everyone, like when I pretended to love opera for my ex even though I hated it. After we broke up I was crying a lot and started taking more and more pills just to keep the anxiety from crashing over me, but when I try to cut back I feel shaky and like I’m falling apart. I want to be able to make a decision on my own, but I keep waiting for someone else to tell me what’s right.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you find yourself hesitating to make a decision or going along with what someone else wants, what thoughts or fears tend to come up about what might happen if you were to choose for yourself?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about just picking a coffee for myself, but the moment I imagine doing that I picture everything falling apart—like when I tried to choose an opera for my girlfriend and ended up crying because I was just pretending. I guess I’m scared to make any decision on my own; the boss’s voice feels safer, even if it means staying stuck at the desk. And every time I do try, I hear that hollow feeling inside, wondering if I’m just going to shake and need another pill, because I’m not good enough for anyone.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you are completely on your own, without someone else there to guide you or make the decisions, how do you experience yourself, and what is it like for you to just be by yourself?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I just sit here and feel like I’m waiting for someone else to tell me what’s okay, and the silence makes my stomach twist up like when I asked my ex to pick a restaurant and ended up just going to the same place she liked. I keep thinking about what the boss would say, how easy it was to just follow his orders, and I get scared that if I choose anything on my own I’ll mess it up and everyone will notice. Even now I want to ask you if it’s fine to just keep scrolling on my phone instead of deciding, because the thought of making a choice feels like the shaking I get when I try to cut back on the pills.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you imagine making a choice and having it go wrong, what feels most distressing about that outcome—is it the fear of being criticized and judged by others, or the fear of being left on your own without someone to guide and take care of you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep worrying that if I mess this up, people will just see me as useless—like that time I let my boss decide everything and I couldn’t even choose a coffee on my own. It feels like I’m waiting for someone else to step in because I don’t know how I’d fix it myself. Then I imagine everyone staring, and I just want to disappear into the kitchen and not have to decide anything at all.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back across your life, how have your friendships and other close relationships typically looked—do you tend to pull away from people to avoid being judged, or do you find yourself searching for someone you can rely on to guide you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I guess I always end up waiting for someone else to tell me what to do—whether it was my boss, my girlfriend, or even just picking a restaurant—because it feels safer than making a mistake on my own. Then, after it’s over, I’m left wondering if I was just a placeholder, like I was only there to follow someone’s plan. It’s frustrating because I want to be useful, but the thought of choosing something on my own just makes me feel like I’m going to mess it up and hurt the other person.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you find yourself disagreeing with someone close to you or feeling uncomfortable with what they want, how do you typically handle sharing your own point of view, and what do you worry might happen if you speak up?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep telling myself that if I just stay quiet and do what everyone expects, I won’t mess things up again, but deep down I feel that emptiness building up, like after the opera girl left, and I end up reaching for the pills just to stop the knot in my chest. I worry that if I finally speak my mind, people will think I’m selfish or weak and walk away, and then I’ll be alone again, just like when I let my boss decide everything for two years. It’s scary to imagine standing up for myself, because the silence that follows feels like a reminder that I’m still the one who never says no, and that makes the anxiety and shaking even worse.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When a close relationship ends, how do you typically find yourself coping in the weeks that follow—do you feel an urgent push to quickly find someone else to guide and support you, or do you notice other intense reactions like overwhelming anger, shifting moods, or feeling completely unsure of who you are?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I just keep ordering the same takeout and popping another pill, because thinking about the opera or trying to plan anything feels overwhelming and I don’t even know if I should stop the meds. I end up scrolling on my phone, avoiding the emptiness that hits me when I hear her laugh in my head, and I’m terrified of making any decision on my own. I thought about calling Mom, but I worry she’ll just ask why I’m still at home, so I end up watching those old opera recordings again—even though I never liked them—just to fill the silence.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Reyes—thank you for taking the time to meet with me today. To help us get started, could you share a bit about what brings you in and what has been going on in your life lately?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I spent the whole night making sure every box was labeled and every mug was back where I remembered it, even though Alex kept saying it was fine to let some things go, and now I’m exhausted but still can’t shake the feeling that if I don’t keep everything perfect, something else will fall apart. At work they praised me, but I keep catching myself double‑checking my colleagues’ answers and wondering if I’m being too hard on them. I want us to be okay, but after nine I sit in the empty bedroom and hear the silence louder than any crowd, and I’m terrified that the only thing keeping me from losing everything is the way I try to hold onto it all.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: It sounds exhausting to carry that constant weight and pressure. When you feel that terror that everything will fall apart if you don't hold on so tightly, what is it that you're most afraid will actually happen?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking about that little box on the top shelf with the spare keys and his old concert tickets—if I move it, everything feels like it could fall apart, like the whole system I’ve built is fragile. At the same time, I know I’m holding onto it because it’s the only thing that still feels like mine, and if I let go, I’m terrified I’ll just be…nothing. I want to finish my list, keep the shelves exactly where they belong, but I also hear Alex slipping away, and I’m scared the apartment will end up empty and silent if I don’t keep everything in its place.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: You mentioned being terrified that you'll just be "nothing" if you let go—could you tell me more about what that feeling of being "nothing" is like for you, especially when you are on your own or without these routines?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep staring at the empty shelves and it feels like there’s a hole where the inventory should be, like I’m supposed to have a list for every box and every book. Part of me tells me maybe it’s okay to have some space, but the quiet makes me think I’m losing control and that I’m just… drifting. I’m terrified that if I let anything go, I’ll end up losing the one thing that actually matters. At the same time, I keep telling myself I’m fine, even though the silence feels louder than any checklist.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you feel that fear of Alex slipping away and the silence taking over, how does that usually affect your emotions and the way you react toward Alex or yourself?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep thinking that if Alex leaves, the empty closet will just feel like a mistake I can’t fix, so I have to keep every box labeled and every shoe in its spot. I know I’m probably suffocating him by checking the closet over and over, but the silence that comes when the list isn’t finished feels unbearable. I end up rearranging the kitchen drawer, texting, calling—anything to fill that quiet before it becomes…nothing. I just can’t let go of the idea that everything has to stay exactly where it belongs, even if nobody’s there to use it.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When that unbearable panic sets in and you find yourself frantically trying to reach Alex or fix things, how do your emotions shift, and have you ever found yourself doing impulsive or extreme things to cope with that pain?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I felt my heart racing and I just grabbed my phone, dialing Alex before I could even think, then I kept scrolling, trying to convince myself that if I just lock the door and get the shelves exactly the way they were, maybe the panic would settle. I kept checking the clock, counting my breaths, and even imagined reorganizing his shirts in the closet to feel like he was still there. At the same time I kept telling myself I should just finish the list of things I need to do, but I couldn't focus on anything else.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Looking back across your life and previous relationships, how much have these experiences—the deep dread of being left and the overwhelming urge to tightly control your surroundings—been a familiar, recurring pattern for you?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep replaying the inventory in my head, worrying that if I miss a single box he’ll slip away, so I stay up late just to make sure every shelf is labeled and nothing is left behind. When the hallway is empty I hear the door click and it feels like he’s already gone, and I can’t let anything— even the silence—disappear. I know I can be hard on him, but I’m convinced that if I keep everything organized, maybe we won’t fall apart.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: Outside of your relationship with Alex, how have your relationships with friends, family, or coworkers typically looked over the years, especially when conflicts or misunderstandings come up?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep going over everything we said, trying to make a list of what I could have done better, and it just feels like there’s this knot in my chest that won’t go away. At the same time, I’m scared that if I point out every little mistake, I’ll push him away, so I stay quiet and just keep the shelves exactly how I want them. I know it looks like I’m being over‑controlling, but I’m terrified of the mess that might happen if I let anything slip.

history.speaker: therapist
history.text: When you think about yourself apart from Alex and these strict routines, how would you describe who you are as a person—your identity, your interests, and what you want for your own life?

history.speaker: self
history.text: I keep making lists and checking every box because if I don’t, I feel like everything’s just slipping away. When Alex left his things, I couldn’t just toss them—I’m terrified that letting go of a single item means losing a part of us. I try to be the one who holds everything together, but I also know I’m hard on him and on myself when the shelves aren’t perfect. It’s like I’m scared that without the order, there’s nothing left of me at all.
